written.myAnswer: Spindle fibres attach to chromosomes at their kinetochores, near the centromeres, and move the sister chromatids towards opposite poles during anaphase.

In animal cells, a cleavage furrow forms at the equator and moves inward to divide the cell. In plant cells, Golgi-derived vesicles fuse at the equator to form a cell plate, which grows outward and develops into the separating wall. The phragmoplast is the structure that guides cell-plate formation.
Sister chromatids separate, and spindle fibres move them towards opposite poles of the cell.
The centrosomes move to opposite sides of the cell and organize the microtubules that form the mitotic spindle.
Mitosis produces new cells that help replace or rebuild tissues during regeneration.

In prophase, chromosomes condense, the nuclear envelope and nucleolus break down, and the spindle forms. In metaphase, chromosomes align at the equator. In anaphase, sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles. In telophase, nuclear envelopes reform, nucleoli reappear, and chromosomes decondense. Cytokinesis then divides the cytoplasm to produce two daughter cells.

In animal cells, a contractile ring creates a cleavage furrow that moves inward and divides the cell. In plant cells, Golgi-derived vesicles fuse at the equator to form a cell plate; the phragmoplast guides its formation as it grows outward and joins the cell membrane.
Mitosis supports growth, replacement of worn-out or damaged cells, regeneration, and asexual reproduction such as budding in Hydra.

If checkpoints fail to prevent cells with errors from dividing, cells may multiply uncontrollably and form tumours. A tumour that invades other tissues is malignant; its spread to other parts of the body is metastasis.
